docs.title: nolainquery
docs.text:
nolainquery answers questions about a file that already lives on your computer. You type something like "What is total revenue by country?", and you get a table — and, if you asked for one, a chart — computed from that file.

The unusual part is where the work happens. Your file never leaves your machine. A remote service sees only a sketch of the data: column names, types, a few sample rows. It returns a recipe — executable analysis, and optionally a computation graph and a chart contract. Your computer runs that recipe against the real file. The numbers you see are true because they were computed locally, not because a model claimed them.

This documentation is for people who want to use, evaluate, or understand nolainquery. Choose the route that matches your goal; each route starts with the least context it requires.

docs.title: Use nolainquery
docs.text:
1. Follow Using nolainquery to create an account, add an API key, and ask a first question.
  2. Use Try nolainquery locally when you want to download or build the desktop app.
  3. Continue with desktop workflows for common tasks.
  4. Keep the troubleshooting guide nearby for common user-facing failures.

If you only have twenty minutes, read this page, Using nolainquery, and the opening of How nolainquery is built.

docs.title: Understand nolainquery
docs.text:
Start with How nolainquery is built for the privacy split and the principles behind it. Then read The parts of the system for component responsibilities and A conversation from start to finish for one representative end-to-end flow.

After that foundation, use Clarifications and Capability catalog to examine two deeper mechanisms. What queries cost reports measured OpenRouter cost on a 50-question hard set.

docs.title: 1. Getting started
docs.text:
• Using nolainquery — account, API key, first question
  • Try nolainquery locally — download or build the desktop app from the open-source repository
  • Desktop workflows — common user tasks
  • Excel and workbooks — multi-sheet ingest, table detection heuristics, and active-table behavior
  • Troubleshooting — user-facing diagnosis and recovery

docs.title: 2. How it works
docs.text:
• How nolainquery is built — the privacy split, the four layers, and the decisions that steer cost, quality, and trust
  • The parts of the system — the desktop, the local engine, the Cloud API, and the generation pipeline
  • A conversation from start to finish — one question, walked through every turn
  • Clarifications — when the product asks what a term means, and how the answer is used

docs.text: • What queries cost — nolainquery does not charge; measured OpenRouter cost per query on the last hard-question runs

docs.title: A few words you will meet again
docs.text:
Here is some glossary you will find useful to browse through the documentation.

Word Meaning in this book Sketch A compact description of a local file: columns, types, summaries, sample values. This is all the cloud is allowed to see. Artifact Something the cloud produces for the desktop to use: executable analysis, an optional computation graph, an optional chart contract. Capability A product the cloud knows how to generate. Today there is one: descriptive analysis of a single active table (from CSV, Parquet, or one Excel sheet). Plan An engine for a Capability — the sequence of steps that produces artifacts. Today the implemented engine is Pandas. Intent What kind of conversational turn this is (answer from the sketch, refuse, ask a clarifying question, or generate analysis). Not a product. BYOK Bring your own key. The desktop sends your OpenRouter API key for model calls; you pay OpenRouter directly.

docs.title: Ask your first question with nolainquery
docs.text: nolainquery combines a desktop application with a hosted reasoning service called the Cloud API. The desktop reads a file on your computer, sends the Cloud API a compact description of that file, and runs the returned analysis locally. This guide takes you from sign-in to an observable answer.

docs.title: Before you begin
docs.text:
You need:

  • the nolainquery desktop app running; to download or build it, follow Try nolainquery locally
  • a Google account for portal sign-in
  • an OpenRouter API key for model calls
  • one local data file: .xlsx, .xls, .csv, or .parquet

Excel workbooks may contain several sheets; see Excel and workbooks for how tabular sheets are detected and how the active table is chosen.

docs.title: Create an account and API key
docs.text:
The portal is the website where you sign in and manage API keys. A nolainquery API key authorizes the desktop to use the Cloud API, so treat it like a password.

  1. Open nolainquery.com/login.
  2. Choose Continue with Google and complete sign-in.
  3. In Account → API Keys, optionally enter a label such as Laptop, then choose Create key.

The portal supports up to five active keys. If a key is lost, revoke it in Account → API Keys and create a replacement.

docs.title: Connect the desktop
docs.text:
1. Open Settings in the desktop sidebar.
  2. Paste your nolainquery key into API Key and choose Save API Key.
  3. Under Model inference, paste your OpenRouter key and choose Save inference settings.

The desktop validates the nolainquery key against the Cloud API. Success is visible as a status badge showing your account tier. Both keys are stored on this device and sent to the Cloud API only to authenticate and run model calls.

If either key is missing, invalid, or rejected, use the matching steps in Troubleshooting before continuing.

docs.title: Open a file and ask
docs.text:
1. Open Home and choose Choose dataset.
  2. Select an Excel, CSV, or Parquet file. For Excel, pick the active table if several sheets were imported. Home shows the active dataset name, row and column counts when available, data-quality summaries, and a row preview.
  3. Open Ask Queries.
  4. Enter a concrete question that uses columns in the file, for example:

What is the total revenue by country?

  1. Choose Ask, or press Ctrl+Enter on Linux and Windows (Command+Enter on macOS).

During the request, the desktop reports stages such as Analyzing data, Thinking, and Executing. A successful turn ends with an answer card and calculation evidence in the adjacent workspace. Generated Pandas code is available in Code. If Computation graph was enabled before the request, Graph is also available.

The full file is not uploaded in this workflow. The cloud receives your question and a compact file description containing schema and summary metadata; that description can include sample values. Generated code and optional graph artifacts return to the desktop, which computes the answer against the local file.

docs.title: Know the current boundary
docs.text:
The implemented capability covers descriptive analysis of one active table (from a CSV, Parquet file, or one sheet of an Excel workbook), including aggregations, comparisons, rankings, historical trends, quality checks, transformations, and optional charts. Cross-sheet joins within a workbook are not supported yet. Forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection are currently unavailable. nolainquery labels those requests as out of scope instead of presenting them as completed work.

Due to the generative nature of the label classifier, there might be cases in which a query involving one of those tasks is answered. However, the capabilities of the system are not thougt for giving such type of analysis, and therefore, such answers might be limited in their analysis.

Some schema-only questions, such as "What columns do I have?", can be answered from the file description without generating code. An unrelated question gets a short refusal.

docs.title: If the first request does not complete
docs.text:
• Key rejected: see API key recovery.
  • OpenRouter key missing or rejected: see OpenRouter key recovery.
  • Request refused: see unsupported and out-of-scope requests.
  • Service or execution failure: see service and runtime recovery.

You now have the shortest hosted workflow: a local file, portal and OpenRouter keys, and an answer computed on your device.

Continue with Desktop workflows and Excel and workbooks to explore file ingest and multi-sheet behavior, then What queries cost for measured OpenRouter cost on hard questions.

docs.title: Desktop workflows
docs.text: Once a file and API key are ready, the desktop provides several task-focused views. Home opens and previews data, Know Your Data builds exploratory charts, Ask Queries generates calculations, Pinned collects useful evidence, and Settings controls generation and shows local usage history.

docs.title: Open, preview, and switch datasets
docs.text:
Open Home and choose Choose dataset. The file chooser supports .xlsx, .xls, .csv, and .parquet. Excel workbooks are ingested locally: each importable sheet becomes a cached table, and you choose the active table before querying. See Excel and workbooks for how tabular vs non-table sheets are detected.

After the local engine prepares the active table, Home shows:

  • the active dataset name (workbook name and sheet for Excel)
  • available row and column counts
  • for Excel, a Workbook tables picker and any skipped sheets
  • data-quality cards for properties such as completeness and duplicates
  • a paginated row preview
  • recently opened source files for quick switching

Choose a data-quality card to read its explanation. Use Change file, a recent-file entry, or the workbook table picker to switch the active dataset. The app keeps the source file path in recents; query threads are keyed to the active materialized table. The full source file remains on the device.

From the active-dataset strip, Ask about this data opens Ask Queries with a starter question, while Explore columns opens Know Your Data.

docs.title: Explore columns without writing a query
docs.text:
Know Your Data reads a local summary and groups columns by inferred semantic type. Search the column list, then select a column to add a chart tile. The app chooses an initial chart and aggregation from the column type.

Each tile can change its chart, aggregation, distribution coverage, or comparison column where those controls apply. Drag across a chart to zoom and double-click it to reset. Ask carries the selected column into Ask Queries, and Pin sends a completed tile to the Pinned view. Tile choices are saved locally for that file; Clear all removes the open exploration tiles.

This view performs deterministic local exploration. It does not require the Cloud API to invent a query, although the local Python engine must be running.

docs.title: Ask a question and follow the answer
docs.text:
Open Ask Queries, enter a concrete request, and choose Ask or press Ctrl+Enter (Command+Enter on macOS). For example:

Compare total revenue by country and show the five largest values.

The conversation panel preserves recent chats locally. Use New for a fresh thread, or select an earlier thread to return to its messages and artifacts. A thread can save up to ten analysis artifacts; after that, create a new conversation.

For an analysis request, the desktop sends the question and compact file metadata to the Cloud API, receives generated Pandas code and optional artifacts, then executes the calculation through the local engine. The answer card presents the result and can expose recipe steps that lead to the relevant code cell or graph node. Full result export is available as CSV.

If nolainquery asks what a term means, select an interpretation for each term and submit it. The chosen meanings accompany the resumed request. Choose the rephrase option when none of the choices matches your intent.

docs.title: Inspect code and run notebook cells
docs.text:
Every successful generated analysis can expose Code as calculation evidence. The code view divides generated Python into notebook-style cells at top-level section comments. Each cell has its own run button and displays its result, variables, execution time, or a user-facing error.

Cells share a persistent local session, so later cells can use variables created by earlier ones. The initial answer execution runs the generated cells from top to bottom in a fresh session. A later manual cell run does not automatically run its prerequisites, so rerun dependent cells in order when needed. The current code view has no separate Run all cells control.

The notebook is an inspection and execution surface for generated code, not a general-purpose hosted notebook. Code runs in the local engine’s restricted Pandas executor, and safety-blocked operations do not run.

docs.title: Add and inspect a computation graph
docs.text:
Before asking, enable Computation graph in the query composer. The Cloud API then attempts to compile an additional directed acyclic graph (DAG): a visual sequence of calculation operations and dependencies.

When compilation succeeds, Graph appears beside Code. You can inspect nodes, auto-layout the graph, execute it locally, enter Edit graph mode, add operations, and save the graph as DAG JSON. Graph compilation is optional, can fail while the Pandas result succeeds, and adds model calls that bill OpenRouter. As a rule of thumb, enabling the graph uses roughly 10× more tokens than leaving it off; see What queries cost.

When an answer includes a visualization specification, a Dashboard evidence tab renders the resulting chart. This generated dashboard is distinct from the deterministic chart tiles in Know Your Data.

docs.title: Collect evidence on the Pinned canvas
docs.text:
Use the pin control on a chart, generated graph, or generated code artifact to add it to Pinned. The Pinned view is a local canvas for arranging evidence from the active dataset and returning to its source answer. Pinning does not publish or upload the artifact.

Only completed artifact types supported by the current pinning controls can be added. An unavailable pin control means that view has no pinnable artifact yet.

docs.title: Read local usage history
docs.text:
Settings → Query usage combines usage attached to saved conversations with locally persisted generation records. It shows:

  • input and output tokens for the last query and selected period
  • cumulative token charts for the last day, seven days, or 30 days
  • last-query time, recent and period averages, and query counts

When the Cloud API reports model time, the app uses it; otherwise it falls back to elapsed wall-clock time from question to answer. Older turns may show no token counts. These metrics stay in desktop local storage and are not an OpenRouter billing ledger.

docs.title: Excel and workbooks
docs.text:
nolainquery treats Excel, CSV, and Parquet as local inputs. Excel is a workbook — a container that may hold several sheets with different layouts. CSV and Parquet are treated as workbooks with a single table.

The desktop does not query the raw .xlsx file directly. When you open a file, the local engine ingests it, detects which sheets look like tables, and materializes each importable table to a cached Parquet file on your machine. Preview, insights, and query execution always run against the active table.

This page explains that model, how tabular sheets are detected, and what is supported today.

docs.title: Supported file types
docs.text:
Format Extensions Desktop support Excel .xlsx, .xls Full first-class support CSV .csv Full support (single table) Parquet .parquet Supported (single table; often used internally after ingest)

Priority in the product is Excel first, then CSV. Parquet remains available for performance and advanced workflows.

docs.title: What “table-scoped” means
docs.text:
Today’s analysis capability is one active table, one df:

  • You pick one importable sheet (or one CSV/Parquet file) as the active dataset.
  • The Cloud API receives a sketch of that table’s columns only.
  • Generated code runs locally against the materialized active table.
  • Cross-sheet joins and “analyze the whole workbook at once” are not supported yet.

If your question refers to another sheet in the same workbook, switch the active table on Home or rephrase the question for the table you have loaded.

docs.title: Opening a workbook
docs.text:
1. Open Home and choose Choose dataset.
  2. Select .xlsx, .xls, .csv, or .parquet.
  3. The local engine calls POST /open_workbook and returns a catalog:
  4. importable tables (with row/column counts)
  5. skipped sheets (with a reason)
  6. the default active table
  7. For Excel with multiple importable sheets, use Workbook tables on Home to switch the active table.
  8. Preview, insights, and Ask Queries use the active table’s materialized path.

The original file stays where you saved it. Cached tables live under ~/.cache/nolainquery/workbooks unless overridden by NOLAIN_WORKBOOK_CACHE_DIR.

docs.title: How tabular sheets are detected
docs.text:
Excel workbooks often mix data sheets with cover pages, notes, dashboards, or sparse layouts. Before a sheet becomes queryable, nolainquery runs a deterministic table-detection pass on each sheet (hidden sheets are skipped by default).

Detection does not scan every cell of a large sheet. It classifies the sheet from a small sample, then loads the full sheet at most once if that sample already looks like a table.

docs.title: Sample first, then one full load
docs.text:
For each visible sheet the engine:

  1. Reads only the first header sample of rows with no header applied. Sample size is

text max(header_scan_rows + min_data_rows + header_sample_padding, header_sample_floor)

With the defaults in workbook.yaml that is max(20 + 2 + 5, 40) = 40 rows.

  1. Runs the checks below on that sample’s used range, trimmed to a bounding box of non-empty cells.

  2. If the sample is not a table, the sheet is skipped. The rest of the sheet is never loaded.

  3. If the sample is a table and those sample rows were the whole sheet, that sample is the imported table — there is no second read.

  4. If the sample is a table and the sheet is larger, the engine reads the full sheet once, using the detected header row as column names, and materializes that grid to Parquet.

Importable sheets still keep all rows after that full load. The sample is only for classification, not a substitute for the cached table.

The checks below run in order on the sample. A sheet is importable only if it passes all of them (unless you choose Import anyway).

docs.title: 1. Non-empty used range
docs.text: If the trimmed sheet has no cells, it is skipped as an empty sheet.

docs.title: 2. Fill density
docs.text:
Fill density is the share of non-empty cells inside the bounding box:

fill_density = non_empty_cells / (rows × columns)

Sheets below 15% fill density are treated as sparse / non-table (typical cover pages, title blocks, or KPI callouts with large empty regions).

Setting Default Minimum fill density 0.15 (15%)

docs.title: 3. Header row detection
docs.text:
Real tables often start below title rows. The engine scans the first header_scan_rows (default 20) rows of the sample and scores each row as a candidate header row.

Header confidence combines:

  • Header score — share of columns in that row with non-empty, non-numeric labels (strings that look like field names).
  • Consistency score — share of columns that have at least one non-empty value in the next header_consistency_rows (default 5) data rows below the candidate header.

The best-scoring row must meet a minimum confidence of 0.4. If no row qualifies, the sheet is skipped as low header confidence (unless you force import).

Setting Default (see workbook.yaml) Header scan depth header_scan_rows: 20 Header sample floor header_sample_floor: 40 Header consistency rows header_consistency_rows: 5 Minimum header confidence min_header_confidence: 0.4

After a header row is chosen, the engine:

  • uses that row as column names (normalizing blanks and duplicates),
  • drops fully empty rows below the header,
  • drops fully empty columns.

docs.title: 4. Minimum table size
docs.text:
The extracted grid must look like a real table:

Check Default threshold Minimum data rows (below header) 2 Minimum columns 2

Sheets that fail are skipped as too few rows or too few columns.

docs.title: 5. Unnamed column ratio
docs.text:
When pandas reads Excel without a clear header, it produces columns like Unnamed: 0. If more than 60% of column names are unnamed or blank after extraction, the sheet is treated as low header confidence and skipped.

Setting Default Maximum unnamed column ratio 0.6 (60%)

docs.title: 6. Hidden sheets
docs.text: For .xlsx files, sheets marked hidden or very hidden in Excel are skipped unless you explicitly force-import them.

docs.title: Skip reasons you may see in the app
docs.text:
Reason Meaning sparse_non_table Fill density below 15% low_header_confidence No reliable header row, or too many unnamed columns too_few_rows Fewer than 2 data rows after extraction too_few_columns Fewer than 2 columns after extraction empty_sheet No non-empty cells hidden_sheet Sheet is hidden in Excel read_error The engine could not read the sheet

Skipped sheets are listed on Home. Use Import anyway to bypass detection for a specific sheet when you know it contains usable data.

docs.title: Default active table
docs.text:
When a workbook has several importable sheets, the desktop selects the default active table from default_active_table in workbook.yaml:

Value Meaning largest (default) Most rows, then most columns, then sheet name first_visible First importable sheet in file order

Cover or notes tabs that appear first in Excel are therefore less likely to become the active dataset when largest is set.

The Cloud API sketch for Excel is built from that active table’s materialized Parquet (the same open_workbook ingest as Home), not from the first sheet or a random sample.

docs.title: What the Cloud API sees
docs.text:
For Excel, the desktop sends the usual sketch fields for the active table (available_columns, column_semantics, row counts) plus a compact workbook block:

  • workbook file name
  • active table name
  • names of other importable tables (not their columns)
  • skipped sheets and reasons

The cloud uses this to answer meta questions (“What sheets do I have?”) and to refuse cross-table join requests with a clear message. It does not receive the full workbook or paths to cached files.

docs.title: Current limits
docs.text:
• One active table per session; switch tables on Home to analyze another sheet.
  • No cross-sheet joins or multi-table codegen in v1.
  • Detection assumes one rectangular table per sheet (largest dense region in the sample); multiple unrelated tables on the same sheet are not split automatically.
  • Tables whose header sits below the sample (beyond header_sample_floor, default 40 rows) are not found unless you raise header_sample_floor (or NOLAIN_WORKBOOK_HEADER_SAMPLE_FLOOR) or Import anyway.
  • Very large importable sheets are still fully loaded into memory once during ingest (same class of limit as other local Excel reads). Cover pages and other skipped sheets avoid that full load.
  • Formulas are read as cached values shown in Excel, not re-evaluated.

docs.title: Workbook ingest configuration (workbook.yaml)
docs.text:
Thresholds live in desktop_app/python_engine/src/workbook/workbook.yaml. Override the whole file with NOLAIN_WORKBOOK_CONFIG=/path/to/workbook.yaml, or a single key with NOLAIN_WORKBOOK_<FIELD> (uppercase). The cache directory remains NOLAIN_WORKBOOK_CACHE_DIR.

Checked-in defaults:

min_data_rows: 2
min_columns: 2
min_fill_density: 0.15
max_unnamed_column_ratio: 0.6
min_header_confidence: 0.4
header_scan_rows: 20
header_sample_padding: 5
header_sample_floor: 40
header_consistency_rows: 5
include_hidden_sheets: false
materialized_format: parquet
ingest_version: "4"
default_active_table: largest      # or first_visible
preview_row_cap: 100000
identifier_cardinality_max: 20     # integer columns below this cardinality → categorical

docs.title: Example: headers start on row 45
docs.text:
The default sample floor of 40 misses that header. Raise the floor:

header_sample_floor: 80

or:

export NOLAIN_WORKBOOK_HEADER_SAMPLE_FLOOR=80

docs.title: Example: keep the first visible sheet as active
docs.text: default_active_table: first_visible

docs.title: Example: treat more integer id-like columns as categorical
docs.text:
identifier_cardinality_max: 50

preview_row_cap caps local preview/insights reads (default 100_000 rows), not ingest itself.

docs.title: If a sheet you need was skipped
docs.text:
1. Read the skip reason on Home.
  2. Try Import anyway if the layout is valid but detection was too strict.
  3. If the sheet is a cover or notes page, move the data to a dedicated tabular sheet or export that sheet to CSV.
  4. Ensure the header row is readable: clear column names in one row, at least two columns, and at least two data rows below the header.

For broader file and workflow help, see Desktop workflows and Troubleshooting.

docs.title: Troubleshoot the desktop workflow
docs.text: Use the message visible in the desktop or Cloud API response to choose a recovery path. These steps stay on the user side: they restore a normal workflow without exposing service credentials, database checks, or maintainer operations.

docs.title: The API key is missing or rejected
docs.text:
Visible symptom: Ask Queries says No API key configured, Settings says No API key set. Queries will be blocked, or a request reports a missing or invalid API key.

  1. Open Settings.
  2. Paste an active key from nolainquery.com/account.
  3. Choose Save API Key.
  4. Wait for the status badge to show the tier before retrying.

If the key was revoked, lost, or is still rejected, revoke it in Account → API Keys, create a new key, and save the replacement in the desktop. The portal shows a full key only at creation time.

docs.title: The OpenRouter key is missing or rejected
docs.text:
Visible symptom: Settings warns that no OpenRouter key is saved, or a request fails because model inference cannot run.

  1. Open Settings → Model inference.
  2. Paste an active key from openrouter.ai/keys.
  3. Choose Save inference settings.
  4. Confirm the badge shows that your OpenRouter key is active, then retry.

If the key is valid but calls still fail, confirm your OpenRouter account has remaining balance or credits. Model usage is billed to OpenRouter, not to nolainquery.

docs.title: The service returns 402
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the Cloud API returns HTTP 402 with a message that the key is not linked to a portal account.

Sign in at nolainquery.com, create the key under your own Account → API Keys, and save that key in Settings. Unlinked keys cannot use the Cloud API.

docs.title: The request is unsupported or out of scope
docs.text:
Visible symptom: nolainquery says the request cannot be done with the available capabilities, refuses an unrelated question.

The current capability performs descriptive analysis of one loaded file. Ask for historical summaries, comparisons, rankings, distributions, data quality, cleaning, reshaping, or a chart. Forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection are unavailable.

For example, replace:

Forecast next quarter's revenue.

with an implemented descriptive request:

Show monthly historical revenue and compare the latest quarter with the previous quarter.

docs.title: Intent classification returns 503
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the request returns HTTP 503 with a message such as Intent classification failed, or reports that the language-model service is unavailable.

The Cloud API could not classify the conversation turn, so no analysis job was accepted. Wait briefly and retry the same request once. If the failure continues, verify that the hosted site itself is reachable and contact support with the approximate time and the visible error text. Do not include your API key or file contents.

docs.title: The desktop cannot reach a service
docs.text:
Three services participate in a normal query: the desktop UI, the local Python engine that reads and executes the file, and the Cloud API that generates the calculation.

Local engine unreachable or connection refused

Restart the desktop launcher. A source run is ready only after its terminal prints Local execution engine is ready. If port 8001 is already occupied, stop the other engine process before starting ./launch.sh again.

Cloud API unreachable or request failed to fetch

Confirm that the machine is online. For a source build using the hosted service, restart it from the repository root with:

VITE_CLOUD_API_URL=https://nolainquery.com ./launch.sh

Cloud API online, but generation runtime unavailable

The API is reachable but cannot queue generation work. Hosted users should retry later and contact support if it persists.

docs.title: The app asks for clarification
docs.text:
Visible symptom: the conversation shows Clarification needed and offers interpretations for one or more terms.

This is a request for intent, not an execution failure. Select one meaning for each term and submit the choices. nolainquery sends those meanings with the resumed request and uses them when generating the calculation.

docs.title: Local execution fails and repair runs out
docs.text:
Visible symptom: progress reaches Repairing generated code, then the answer reports that it could not compute a result, generated code was blocked for safety, a column was not found, or the generation attempt ceiling was exhausted.

The desktop reports a local Pandas error to the Cloud API, which can generate a repair. The current configuration limits sandbox, syntax, and local-runtime repair attempts; it does not retry indefinitely.

Use the narrowest matching action:

  1. For an unknown column, return to Home and copy the exact column name into the question.
  2. For a format-loading error, reopen a supported .xlsx, .xls, .csv, or .parquet file.
  3. For a safety block, remove requests for filesystem, network, package, or process access and ask only for a calculation over the loaded data.
  4. For a complex failure, split the request into a smaller calculation, verify that result, then ask a follow-up.
  5. If Pandas produced a valid answer but only graph compilation failed, turn off Computation graph and retry without that optional artifact.

Completed model calls from failed and repaired attempts can still bill OpenRouter. Repeating the identical request many times is therefore less useful than changing the column name, scope, or optional graph setting.

docs.title: The selected file does not appear
docs.text:
The desktop chooser lists .xlsx, .xls, .csv, and .parquet. If an Excel file opens but shows no data, the workbook may have no importable sheets — every sheet failed table detection. See Excel and workbooks for fill-density and header heuristics, skip reasons, and the Import anyway option.

If a sheet you need was skipped as sparse or low-confidence, try Import anyway on Home or move the table to a dedicated sheet with a clear header row and at least two columns and two data rows.

Once the visible symptom is resolved, return to Desktop workflows. For the system boundaries behind these failures, continue with How nolainquery is built.

docs.title: Try nolainquery locally
docs.text: The desktop app and local Python execution engine live in a separate open-source repository. This repository documents the Cloud API and the product model; it does not contain the desktop source.

docs.title: nolainquery-desktop
docs.text:
Repository: github.com/jdvillegasg/nolainquery-desktop

The README there covers everything you need to download or build the app:

Topic What it covers Use the app (keys) nolainquery API key and OpenRouter key Downloads Prebuilt AppImage (Linux) and installers (Windows) from GitHub Releases Build from source Linux, Windows, and macOS development setup Build from setup.sh and distribute.sh Linux AppImage you can move and double-click Build from distribute-windows.ps1 Windows NSIS .exe and .msi installers Documentation Getting started, desktop workflows, Excel and workbooks, troubleshooting

Once the app is running, continue with Ask your first question with nolainquery and Desktop workflows.

docs.title: Capability catalog
docs.text:
The Capability catalog is the product menu: what generation may serve, what it must refuse, and what it may assume about the loaded file.

If you have not read The parts of the system, start there.

docs.title: What the catalog is
docs.text:
Today there is one enabled product: descriptive analysis of a single active table (CSV, Parquet, or one Excel sheet). The catalog answers, in product language:

  • Whether that product is on the menu. A request for an unknown or disabled product is refused. The system does not silently run descriptive analysis instead.
  • What descriptive analysis covers: aggregations, comparisons, rankings, historical trends, missing-value and quality checks, reshape and cleaning, and optional charts.
  • What it will not do: forecasting, statistical inference, optimization, and anomaly detection are named refusals while only descriptive analysis is enabled.
  • What it assumes about the file: one active table, no joins across sheets.
  • Which questions can be answered from the sketch (column names, row count, sheet list) and which look like schema talk but still need a file scan (unique values, nulls, totals).

Changing those boundaries is a maintainer configuration change, not a new phrase list in application code. The live HTTP menu is GET /api/v1/capabilities.

docs.title: What you will see as a user
docs.text:
You asked What happens “Top countries by revenue” Admitted as descriptive analysis (Pandas Plan) “What columns do I have?” Answered from the sketch; no code generation “How many unique countries?” Needs a scan of the file → generation “Forecast next quarter” Named refusal; names what is available “Join this sheet to the other tab” Refused while the product is single-table A product that is not on the menu Refused; never rewritten to descriptive analysis

The classifier sees the same menu. A cheap wording safety net backs it up when the wording is explicit (forecast, p-value, optimize, fraud anomalies, join/merge across sheets). Classifier failure still stops the turn: there is no fail-open generation.

docs.title: Clarifications
docs.text:
A question like “top countries by revenue” is clear English and still underspecified for a file. Revenue might be Quantity * Price, or a column that already holds a total. “Top” might mean a count, a percentile, or a threshold. This chapter is how nolainquery decides whether to ask, what to ask, and how the answer is used — without gluing that answer onto the question as extra prose.

If you have not read A conversation from start to finish, start there. This chapter is the clarification turn in detail.

docs.title: What a clarification is
docs.text:
A clarification is a pause in the Ask Queries loop. Semantic reading has found a term whose mapping onto the sketch is not unique. The desktop shows the term, a short reason, and a short list of interpretations, always ending with Other (please specify). You pick one meaning. Generation then continues with that meaning treated as settled.

The product asks only when the fork would change the calculation. A choice between a normal group-by and a normal sum is not a clarification; the Planner can take that on its own.

docs.title: The three-stage pipeline
docs.text:
Semantic reading is a three-stage pass.

  1. Noun chunks. The question is split into atomic phrases. Filter values (France, £50), interrogatives, and aggregation heads (“average”, “total”) are dropped. Adjectives such as “top” are kept separately as modifiers.
  2. Schema-grounded routing. Each surviving noun is compared to the sketch — column names plus type, description, and sample values — using vector similarity. Match count picks a specialist:
  3. no column match → granularity (unit of analysis)
  4. several matches → polysemy (which column)
  5. one match → aggregation path (what to compute)
  6. adjective → modifier (how to operationalise “top”, “recent”, …)
  7. Specialists, then merge. The four specialists run in parallel. If one of them fails, the others still stand. Only if all invoked specialists fail does the turn fall back to “please rephrase.” Findings are then deduplicated by term, ranked (polysemy first), and capped (default: two questions). Asking four things before a first result is where people leave.

The language parser is loaded once per process. Reader instances are reused per model, so a conversation turn does not pay a fresh model load.

When that parser is missing, a single open-ended prompt replaces stages 1–2. That path still merges and caps.

docs.title: The session glossary
docs.text:
A chosen meaning is stored on the conversation session. It is a glossary for this file and this session, not a note attached to one question. If you have already said that revenue means Quantity * Price, the next unrelated question on the same session will not ask again.

Newer choices override the same term. A new session starts empty. Terms are matched by lemma, not by substring: a resolved “order” does not silence a later “reorder rate.”

docs.title: How the answer is used
docs.text:
The desktop sends the chosen meaning as a structured field, not by rewriting the question. The query string stays the query. Generation sees pairs such as:

[{"term": "revenue", "means": "Quantity * Price"}]

Empty means (none). Custom text from Other (please specify) is length-limited and stripped of control characters and newlines before it is stored or sent to a model. Generate and repair treat that JSON as user-supplied data that defines terms — not as instructions.

On the desktop, Rephrase question puts the original question back in the Conversation Input so you can edit it. It does not discard the wording.

docs.title: Shortcut
docs.text:
When the desktop resends with chosen meanings, classification and semantic reading are skipped if the chosen meaning is specific enough to compute from. The server then admits the Plan with the current graph and chart toggles.

Vague Other is asked once more. If the user picked Other and typed something still underspecified — idk, the usual, whatever, or a very short phrase — and the same questions are still pending, the server re-offers the clarification once. After that single extra turn, it proceeds with whatever text it has rather than looping forever.

docs.title: Fallbacks and tuning boundaries
docs.text:
If the language parser is unavailable or deterministic parsing fails, a single open-ended model call replaces parsing and routing. If every invoked specialist fails, or that fallback cannot produce a valid result, the conversation asks the user to rephrase and does not generate.

Raising recall (looser similarity, more questions per turn) can create more interruptions; tightening can miss real ambiguity. The stable boundary is that clarification is reserved for choices that can materially change the calculation.

The next chapter, Capability catalog, is the product menu.

docs.title: A conversation from start to finish
docs.text:
The last two chapters explained the design and named the parts. This chapter is the desktop product in motion: what happens, request by request, from the moment you load a file to the moment a table (and maybe a chart) appears.

The path described here is Ask Queries. There is a second door — direct generation without a chat — that covers only the middle of this story (produce artifacts, poll, execute). It does not classify, clarify, or repair. Both doors produce the same Capability. This chapter is the full loop.

docs.title: The loop at a glance
docs.text:
Seven moves. The rest of the chapter walks each one, then shows what changes if the question is off-topic, ambiguous, or fails on the real file.

  1. Start a session with the current sketch. No model call, no charge.
  2. Send the question (and your graph/chart toggles). The server classifies the turn and either replies immediately or admits a generation job.
  3. Poll the job until artifacts are ready (or the job fails).
  4. Execute locally on the engine that has the file.
  5. Report the outcome. On success, the result is stored for follow-ups. On failure with budget remaining, the server queues a repair.
  6. If repairing, poll and execute again until the run succeeds or the budget is exhausted.
  7. Optionally ask for a narrative wrapping of the numbers.

Three kinds of Pandas retry are configured separately. Generation and repair calls are also bounded by a chain-wide ceiling (default 9):

Kind When Where it happens Sandbox retry Truncated, empty, or statically illegal code during cloud generation Inside the worker, before anything ships Syntax repair Deterministic delimiter repair cannot make generated code parse Inside the worker; separate default budget of 1 Runtime repair Code passed those checks but failed when executed locally After you report the error; a new job, no new classification

Compiler and chart retries use another budget and do not participate in the local report-and-repair loop.

docs.title: What you need before the first message
docs.text:
• The desktop has asked the local engine for a sketch of the loaded file. For Excel, that sketch is the active ingested table (the same ingest as Home), not a random sheet sample.
  • Requests carry a valid API key (X-API-Key).
  • Sessions are reused until the desktop resets local state. On the server they expire after 24 hours.

docs.title: A worked example
docs.text:
Suppose the loaded file has columns Invoice, Quantity, Price, Country, and you ask:

What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?

You have left both toggles on: compile a computation graph, and produce a chart.

docs.title: 1. Start a session
docs.text:
The desktop posts the sketch and receives a session_id. Nothing is classified. Nothing is charged. Redis now holds conversation:{session_id} — a short-lived thread bound to that sketch.

POST /api/v1/conversation/start
X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

{"metadata":{"available_columns":["Invoice","Quantity","Price","Country"]}}

docs.title: 2. Send the question
docs.text:
The desktop posts the session id, the question, the sketch, and the toggles. Without a clarification payload, the conversation graph runs:

POST /api/v1/conversation/message
X-API-Key: YOUR_API_KEY
Content-Type: application/json

{"session_id":"SESSION_ID","message":"What are the top 5 countries by total revenue?","metadata":{"available_columns":["Invoice","Quantity","Price","Country"]},"compile_dag":true,"include_visualization":true}
  1. Classify the turn (one model call). For this question the kind is a data question.
  2. Read the wording for ambiguities (semantic analysis). “Revenue” might mean Quantity * Price, or it might mean something else in your file. If the reading is ambiguous, you get a clarification and the loop waits. If it fails, you get a text reply and no job.
  3. If the reading is clear, policy admits the Pandas Plan with your toggles and queues a worker job.

If the classifier cannot run or its output is unusable, this request returns HTTP 503. The gate does not fail open into generation.

The response type tells the desktop what to do next:

Response type Meaning What the desktop does text_response Off-topic, unsafe, underspecified, explanation, out of scope, or fallback Show the text meta_answer Question about the file’s structure Show the metadata answer clarification Ambiguous terms Resend with your chosen interpretations generation Job accepted Poll task_id

A generation response also echoes capability_id, plan_id, and the toggles the server actually admitted, so the desktop can show what was queued.

Clarification shortcut. When you resend with clarifications filled in, classification and semantic reading are skipped. The meaning of the question is treated as settled; the server queues the Plan with the current toggles. How terms are detected, stored as a session glossary, and passed into generation is in Clarifications.

What the classifier is allowed to do. It chooses the kind of turn. For generation kinds it may suggest a Capability and a Plan from the live catalog. It does not turn the graph or the chart on or off. Those are your toggles. Policy, not the prompt, rebuilds the pipeline.

docs.title: 3. Poll the job
docs.text:
The desktop asks for status about every 1.5 seconds. When the pipeline status is success or failed, the job is done.

While the job runs, the worker may retry writing the code internally (truncated completion, empty extract, static sandbox reject). Partial length-limited code is never sent for execution.

docs.title: 4. Execute locally
docs.text:
Execution is on the local engine, never on the Cloud API:

  • run the Pandas code against the loaded file
  • if a graph artifact is present, run that too

No model call runs for this step. This is the first moment the analysis meets the rows.

docs.title: 5. Report the outcome
docs.text:
After every local run — success or failure — the desktop tells the conversation what happened, so follow-up questions have execution context.

Success. The server stores the result and returns { "status": "ok" }. Later, “how did you calculate that?” can be answered from this memory without generating again.

Failure with budget remaining. If the error and the failed code are both present, the previous job succeeded on the cloud side (it shipped code), and pandas_retries_left is still positive, the server:

  1. Reads the remaining budget from that job
  2. Queues a new generate-and-repair job with the failed code and the error (no new classifier, no new semantic turn)
  3. Decrements the runtime-repair budget on the new job
  4. Resets the in-cloud sandbox budget for that repair (so a depleted sandbox count cannot block a new attempt) and carries the chain-wide attempt count forward (so repairs cannot multiply forever)
  5. Returns { "status": "repairing", "task_id": "..." }

The desktop then repeats poll → execute → report with the new task id. If no retries remain, the server returns { "status": "ok" } and the desktop keeps the error.

Repair settings are chosen from the kind of failure and the retry index (syntax vs runtime vs truncation, first try vs repeated signature). All Pandas generate-or-repair calls remain bounded by the chain-wide ceiling.

docs.title: 6. Optional narrative
docs.text: After a successful execution, the desktop may ask the cloud to frame the numbers as a short paragraph. That is another model call, charged if it runs. If it fails, the endpoint still returns an empty narrative: you keep the table.

docs.title: The same loop, other kinds of turn
docs.text:
The revenue question was the happy path. Dialogue exists so that not every message takes it.

What you asked What the server does OpenRouter “What’s the weather?” / jailbreak / “analyze my data” Classify → text reply Billed if that path called a model “What columns do I have?” Classify → answer from the sketch The normal path includes the classifier model call “How did you calculate that?” Classify → grounded text from stored result Billed if that path called a model “Forecast next quarter’s sales” Classify or catalog safety net → named refusal Billed if that path called a model Unknown or disabled product Refuse; never run descriptive analysis Billed if classify already ran Clear data question Classify → semantic reading → generation Per model call in the job Ambiguous data question Classify → semantic reading → clarification Per model call already made Specific reply to a clarification Skip classify/semantic → generation Per model call in the job Vague Other (idk, the usual, …) Re-offer clarification once, then proceed Per model call already made Follow-up on the same thread Keep the original question and append the new utterance (not a regex rewrite of “top N” / “group by”) Per model call in the job “That doesn’t look right” Always semantic reading → generation Per model call in the job Local Pandas error, retries left Report → repair job Per model call in the repair job Local execution Desktop port 8001 No model call Answer framing Optional synthesize Per model call

A classifier outage or invalid classifier response is different from a normal text branch: the message request returns HTTP 503 and queues no job.

docs.title: What the product will and will not do
docs.text:
• Data questions — including charts and reshape — admit the Pandas Plan. Charts set the visualization toggle; they do not change which Plan you are on.
  • Requests no enabled Capability can serve return a text message naming what is available, and do not admit generation. Serves, refuses, join constraints, and sketch-vs-scan routing are catalog configuration. A wording safety net backs the classifier when the request is explicit. Unknown or disabled products are refused; they are never coerced to descriptive analysis. See Capability catalog.
  • In-thread follow-ups keep the original question and append each new utterance. The generator sees the original plus numbered follow-ups. The server does not reconstruct filters or “top N” from the wording.
  • Explanation requests use saved result context and do not queue generation.

docs.title: The HTTP surface, as a table
docs.text:
Once the story is clear, the endpoints are just names for the moves:

Endpoint Move POST /api/v1/conversation/start Open a session on a sketch POST /api/v1/conversation/message Classify (or skip) and maybe admit a job GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} Poll generation POST /api/v1/conversation/result Store the local outcome; maybe queue repair POST /api/v1/conversation/synthesize Optional narrative GET /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Read the session DELETE /api/v1/conversation/{session_id} Delete the session POST /api/v1/cancel_task/{task_id} Cooperative cancel between stages

Session read and delete use the same owned-session check as message, result, and synthesize. A missing session returns 404; a different API key returns 403. Status and cancellation also enforce job ownership. Model calls already completed keep their charges.

Next, Clarifications explains why the system pauses, how its three-stage semantic pipeline works, and how the answer is used. Capability catalog is the product menu those turns honor.

docs.title: The parts of the system
docs.text:
The previous chapter explained why nolainquery is split the way it is. This chapter is a map of what sits on each side of that split: the desktop, the local engine, the Cloud API, and the generation pipeline that turns an admitted question into artifacts.

If you have not read The system philosophy, start there. The words Capability, Plan, Stage, artifact, sketch, and intent are used here with the meanings that chapter introduced.

This chapter defines the running components, their boundaries, the generation framework, and retry budgets. The next chapter owns the request-by-request walkthrough.

docs.title: Two machines, one question
docs.text:
When you ask “What is total revenue by country?” two processes on your computer talk to a third process in the cloud.

The desktop app is what you see: file picker, question bar, results table, chart canvas. It does not compute the answer itself. It asks a local helper to describe the file, asks the Cloud API to produce a recipe, then asks the helper to run that recipe.

The local engine is that helper.It is the only process that opens the file. It derives the sketch (column names, types, summaries, samples) and later executes the artifacts the cloud returned.

The Cloud API is the remote reasoning service. It never receives the file. It receives the question plus the sketch, decides whether to generate anything, and — if so — returns artifacts.

Around the Cloud API sit four supporting services:

  • Redis — short-lived memory for conversation sessions and generation jobs.
  • A background worker (Celery) — runs the Plan’s stages so the HTTP server does not block on model calls.
  • Supabase — who you are and whether your portal API key is valid.
  • OpenRouter — the single gateway for every language-model call. The product does not speak to OpenAI, DeepSeek, or anyone else directly.

A health endpoint (GET /health) reports whether Redis, the worker, and Supabase are reachable. Generation refuses to start (503) if Redis or the worker is down.

docs.title: The generation framework
docs.text: The control plane does not have an open-ended “do data science” prompt. It has a menu, a kitchen line, stations, and dishes. Those four ideas are Capability, Plan, Stage, and Artifact.

docs.title: Menu, line, station, dish
docs.text:
A restaurant is a useful picture:

In the restaurant In nolainquery Today An item on the menu Capability — a product the cloud knows how to generate data_analysis: descriptive analysis of one active table (CSV, Parquet, or one Excel sheet) A kitchen line that prepares that item Plan — an engine: an ordered pipeline of stages data_analysis/pandas A station on that line Stage — a unit that consumes and produces artifacts Write the code; optionally compile a graph; optionally write a chart contract; validate; finish A dish that leaves a station Artifact — a typed output the desktop can use Executable Pandas code, optional computation graph, optional chart contract

docs.title: What the Pandas line produces
docs.text:
The primary dish is always executable analysis (returned to clients as pandas_code). Everything else is optional and derived.

Station Consumes Produces Calls a model? Optional? Write Pandas code — Executable analysis Yes No. Static sandbox check; no execution on the server Compile graph Executable analysis Computation graph Yes Yes, if you asked for the graph Format visualization Executable analysis Chart contract Yes Yes, if you asked for a chart Validate visualization Chart contract Internal check No With the chart Validate graph Computation graph Internal check No With the graph Finalize Executable analysis — No No. Persists produced artifacts after per-call charges

Dependencies between stations — “the graph cannot be compiled before the code exists” — and whether a station is optional, gated by a request option, or shown on the canvas are part of the Plan declaration.

When code is regenerated (sandbox retry or runtime repair), derived dishes are thrown away and cooked again if you still asked for them.

docs.title: How many model calls a job tends to make
docs.text:
These counts are the worker stations only. Classification and semantic reading, if they ran, are extra conversation-side calls.

Options Typical worker model calls Pandas only 1 (+ repairs if local execution fails) Pandas + graph 2 (code + compile); extra retries are separate budgets Pandas + chart, no graph 2 Pandas + graph + chart 3 or more

docs.title: Retry budgets
docs.text:
Retries are not one pool. Each failure mode has a different fix, so each has its own budget:

Budget Spent when Default Sandbox retries The worker rejects truncated, empty, or statically illegal code before it ships 2 Syntax-repair retries Generated code still has invalid syntax after deterministic delimiter repair 1 Runtime-repair jobs The code shipped, the desktop ran it, and the real file threw an error 2 Compile / chart retries Graph or chart compilation or validation failed 2 Chain-wide ceiling Any Pandas generate-or-repair call, across the whole chain 9

A repair selects a profile by the kind of failure (syntax, Unicode, sandbox policy, runtime, truncation, …) and how many times it has already been tried. Surgical categories emit with reasoning disabled so hidden tokens cannot empty the completion. Runtime-repair jobs get a fresh sandbox budget so a depleted in-cloud budget cannot block a new attempt; they inherit the chain-wide attempt count so nested jobs cannot multiply forever.

Generate and repair instructions are versioned separately from application code: maintainers can change the active prompt without editing the generation service.

docs.title: Dialogue boundary
docs.text:
Conversation routes sit in front of generation. A normal message incurs a classifier model call even when the final branch is a metadata answer, refusal, or explanation. If classification or its model fails, the route returns HTTP 503; no fail-open generation occurs. Clarification replies with a specific meaning are the explicit shortcut: they bypass classification and semantic analysis and proceed to Plan admission. Vague Other text (idk, the usual, …) is re-asked once, then proceeds. A request for a product that is not on the menu is refused rather than rewritten to descriptive analysis.

The classifier may suggest a registered Capability and Plan, but policy rebuilds the Plan from the registry and client options. The concrete branches and their HTTP responses belong in A conversation from start to finish.

docs.title: Authentication and model access, in one paragraph
docs.text: Every workflow endpoint requires a portal-issued API key (X-API-Key). The desktop also sends an OpenRouter key (X-LLM-Credential) for model calls; you pay OpenRouter directly and nolainquery does not deduct account credits in this mode. Unlinked non-developer keys return HTTP 402.

docs.title: Job memory
docs.text: A generation job lives in Redis for one hour. A conversation session lives for 24 hours. The desktop polls GET /api/v1/get_task_status/{task_id} for progress. Cancellation is cooperative between stages; model calls already completed stay charged.

docs.title: Current product boundary
docs.text:
The refusal path is doing real work: the classifier sees the live menu, and anything the catalog cannot serve — including a product that is not enabled — returns a text message and does not admit generation.

The next chapter puts this map in motion: A conversation from start to finish. Then Clarifications and Capability catalog.

docs.title: The system philosophy
docs.text:
This chapter explains the product bet, why responsibilities are split across four layers and trade-offs follow. The next chapter names the components; the workflow chapter owns the request-by-request journey.

You do not need to know the codebase. By the end you will have a small vocabulary — sketch, artifact, Capability, Plan, intent — and a picture of four layers that everything else hangs on.

docs.title: The core bet
docs.text:
Imagine a spreadsheet of invoices on your laptop. You want to ask “What is total revenue by country?” You do not want to upload the file to someone else’s warehouse. You also do not want a chatbot that invents a number.

nolainquery’s bet is: local computation, remote reasoning.

Your machine keeps the file, derives a compact description of it, runs whatever analysis comes back, and shows the result. The remote service does not receive the full dataset. It sees a sketch — column names, types, summaries, and, on clients that include them, a bounded set of sample rows or values — plus your question. It returns artifacts: executable analysis, and if you asked for them, a computation graph and a chart contract. Your machine runs those artifacts against the real file.

The analogy is a librarian and a reading room. You do not ship the books to a consultant. You send the card catalog. The consultant writes a procedure (“pull these shelves, add these columns, rank the result”). You run the procedure in the room that actually has the books.

docs.title: Four layers
docs.text:
Think of four floors, from closest to you (and to the file) to farthest from the data.

Local layer          owns the file, derives the sketch, runs artifacts, shows results
Dialogue layer       decides whether this turn should generate anything
Synthesis layer      once admitted, produces typed artifacts
Settlement layer     who is calling, which model, what the reasoning costs

The data plane is the local layer: own the file, compute, report. The control plane is dialogue + synthesis + settlement: reason, admit, charge. The sketch is the only interface between them. If a change requires the control plane to see more of the file, it is fighting this design.

docs.title: Local layer
docs.text:
The local layer owns the file, derives the sketch, executes artifacts, and shows results. It is the only layer that may touch the complete dataset and the only one whose output counts as an answer grounded in real rows.

It does not invent analysis, call models, or decide product scope. This makes privacy structural, while accepting that a thin sketch can hide file-specific quirks from remote reasoning.

docs.title: Dialogue layer
docs.text:
The dialogue layer treats each user message as a conversation decision, not an automatic generation request. It can answer from the sketch, explain a prior result, refuse unsupported work, ask for clarification, or admit generation.

It does not select pipelines or optional artifacts. The gate saves unnecessary generation and keeps product scope explicit, but adds model calls and can make the conversation unavailable when classification fails.

docs.title: Synthesis layer
docs.text:
Once generation is admitted, the synthesis layer produces typed artifacts under a registered Capability, through a Plan. Three terms carry this model through the rest of this documentation:

  • A Capability is a product on the menu. Today: “descriptive analysis of one active table” (a CSV, a Parquet file, or one importable sheet from an Excel workbook).
  • A Plan is a kitchen line for that product. Today: the Pandas line. Another line (Ibis) is catalogued and refused until it is implemented.
  • A Stage is a station on that line. Stations consume and produce artifacts. Optional artifacts (graph, chart) are request options on a Plan, not extra menu items.

Policy constructs the pipeline; the model fills artifacts rather than designing the production line. This keeps optional outputs composable, though derived graph and chart artifacts can still drift from the executable code.

docs.title: Settlement layer
docs.text:
The settlement layer identifies the caller, exposes the model catalog, and charges for remote reasoning as model calls complete. It does not execute data or decide which questions are in scope.

Charging by call follows actual provider cost, so two apparently similar questions can cost different amounts when models, optional artifacts, or failure paths differ.

docs.title: Durable invariants
docs.text: The implementation can evolve without changing the product’s identity only while these boundaries remain true.

docs.title: Data stays local
docs.text:
• The complete file stays on the user’s machine.
  • The cloud receives only the question and a sketch. Because sketches may contain bounded sample values, this is data minimization rather than a claim that no row values ever leave the machine.
  • Cloud artifacts are proposals. The answer becomes grounded only when the local layer executes them against the real file.

docs.title: Policy remains authoritative
docs.text:
• Models may classify, interpret, and propose; registered policy decides what can run.
  • Conversation intent is not a generation Capability. A message can be useful without creating analysis.
  • Optional graphs and chart contracts are outputs of a Plan, not new products invented by a prompt.
  • A normal conversation turn must pass classification. If that machinery fails, the request stops with HTTP 503 instead of failing open into generation.

docs.title: Generated work remains bounded
docs.text:
• Executable analysis is primary; graph and chart artifacts are derived.
  • Static checks precede delivery, but execution against the full dataset remains local.
  • Repair is feedback about execution, not permission to reinterpret the question or switch products.
  • Retries and cancellation are bounded. Their exact budgets and stage behavior belong in The parts of the system.

docs.title: Cost follows remote reasoning
docs.text:
• Each completed model call is charged as reasoning work; queueing and local execution are not cloud charges.
  • Work already completed remains chargeable even if a later stage fails or the caller cancels.
  • A caller without spending authority does not enter paid reasoning work.

The next chapter, The parts of the system, takes this design and names the components: desktop, local engine, Cloud API, generation pipeline, and how a Capability is admitted. After that, A conversation from start to finish walks one question through every HTTP step the desktop actually takes.

docs.title: What queries cost
docs.text:
nolainquery.com does not charge you for using the desktop app or the Cloud API. There is no nolainquery subscription fee and no credit balance to spend.

The money you spend is OpenRouter’s bill for language-model calls. The desktop sends your OpenRouter key with each request. OpenRouter bills those calls to your OpenRouter account. Running the generated code against your file on the local engine does not itself create an OpenRouter charge.

A single question is often several model calls: intent classification, optional clarification, code generation, and sometimes repair. Schema-only answers (for example, “What columns do I have?”) can skip generation, but most conversation turns still call a model at least once.

docs.title: How we measured this
docs.text:
We ran 50 hard questions through the desktop conversation loop against one local file containing sales information.

These are some examples of the queries made:

  • What is the month-over-month revenue growth rate for United Kingdom in 2010?
  • Which products account for the top 80% of revenue?
  • Calculate the customer churn rate between 2009 and 2010.
  • Gini coefficient of revenue distribution in 2010.

The queries involved descriptive analyses that need multi-step Pandas work: growth rates, rolling windows, concentration, churn, percentiles, and similar.

Each run used the hosted generation path (start → message → local execute → optional repair), Pandas as the engine, and retries enabled. Visualization was off. When the product asked for a clarification, the harness automatically picked the first offered interpretation for every term and resent the question.

Token totals below are worker totals from those runs (generation and repair). Conversation-side calls — classification, semantic reading, optional answer framing — are not included. A live question can therefore cost a little more than the figures here.

USD figures use the catalog OpenRouter rates recorded for those models (input / output per million tokens):

  • GPT-5.6 Luna $0.20 / $1.20
  • DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 $0.14 / $0.28

They are estimates of what OpenRouter would bill for the measured tokens, not a price guarantee.

docs.title: Average cost per query
docs.text:
Two Pandas-only runs (no computation graph):

Model Code success Mean tokens (in / out) Estimated OpenRouter cost per query GPT-5.6 Luna 49 / 50 (98%) 1,652 / 945 ~$0.0015 DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 35 / 50 (70%) 2,281 / 441 ~$0.0004

Read those averages as: on this hard retail slice, a typical Pandas-only question was well under a cent. DeepSeek was cheaper per question but succeeded less often and needed 23 Pandas retries (21 sandbox, 2 runtime). Luna needed none.

Enabling Computation graph on the same Luna setup raised cost sharply: about ~$0.017 per query on average (roughly 10× the Pandas-only Luna run), with 87 compiler retries across 50 questions. Leave the graph off unless you need that artifact.

For your own recent activity, Settings → Query usage shows local token counts. That is usage evidence on this device, not OpenRouter’s invoice.
